web_evidence.title: The Goldfinch: A Novel — excerpt
web_evidence.note: A sustained opening excerpt, reproduced with Little, Brown’s permission, has the narrator recount his own Amsterdam predicament, memories, mother’s death, and writing in persistent first person.

web_evidence.title: The Goldfinch: Full Book Analysis
web_evidence.note: The whole-book analysis explicitly says everything is told in first person from twenty-seven-year-old Theo’s viewpoint and that Theo narrates throughout the novel.

web_evidence.title: Main Characters in D. Tartt’s Prose: Exploring the Hero
web_evidence.note: This scholarly analysis identifies Theo as the main character functioning as narrator, describes the confessional narrator-reader relationship, and says other characters are seen through Theo’s eyes.

web_evidence.title: Writing the Self: The Written and Visual Art of Self-Portraiture in the Fiction of Donna Tartt
web_evidence.note: The scholarly thesis analyzes Theo’s narrative as his written self-portrait and treats him as the participant who selects, interprets, and recounts his life events.

web_evidence.title: The Goldfinch Book Club Kit
web_evidence.note: The library-hosted author interview calls Theo the novel’s narrator; Tartt explains that the narrator’s metaphors reveal Theo’s mind and perspective.

Searched “The Goldfinch narration first person Theo Decker scholarly”; opened the RUDN journal article and the Södertörn University repository thesis.

Searched publisher and library sources; Hachette’s product page advertised an excerpt but its accessible text did not expose diagnostic prose, while the St. Albert Public Library kit reproduced an author interview discussing Theo as narrator.
Ran targeted searches for alternating narration and whole-book structure; no credible evidence of sustained base narration outside Theo’s first-person account was found.
person_note: The quotes repeatedly expose Theo as a participating narrator through narratorial “I,” “me,” and “my” across memories, scenes, and present reflection. Generic “you/we,” dialogue, gnomic statements, and the Nietzsche epigraph were not treated as competing narrative persons; third-person descriptions of other characters were unmarked unless a first-person frame was visible. The authorized opening excerpt independently confirms sustained first-person narration, while whole-book critical and scholarly sources identify Theo as the narrator throughout. No evidence supports autonomous sections in another person, so the controlling label is FIRST with high confidence.
